blocks.title: Electrolytic cell
blocks.text: An electrolytic cell is a device that converts electrical energy into chemical energy through a process called electrolysis. It consists of two electrodes, typically of metal or another conductor, immersed in an electrolyte, a substance containing free ions that carry electric current.

When a direct current is applied, one electrode becomes negatively charged (the cathode) and the other positively charged (the anode). Positive ions in the electrolyte migrate to the cathode, where they gain electrons (reduction), while negative ions move to the anode, where they lose electrons (oxidation). This movement of ions and transfer of electrons produces chemical changes at the electrodes, converting electrical energy into chemical energy. Electrolytic cells are used in the electrolysis of sodium chloride to produce sodium metal and chlorine gas, in the refining and plating of metals, and in the production of chemicals such as caustic soda; electrolysis also produces non-metals such as chlorine and purifies metals.

In the electrolysis cell of Figure 10.1 the electrolyte is the compound that is decomposed, either a molten ionic compound or a concentrated aqueous solution of ions; the electrodes, of carbon (graphite) or metal, conduct electricity to and from the electrolyte, the anode being the positive electrode and the cathode the negative; and the power supply must be direct current. The actual structure of the cell varies with the element extracted.
